figures.caption: Figure 1. Surgical procedures are hierarchically structured. A gastric bypass decomposes into 12 phases containing 46 steps. For surgical AI, current video-language models embed all levels in a flat space and evaluate each independently, ignoring underlying structure. To address this problem, we introduce (i) a hierarchyaware evaluation suite and (ii) a hyperbolic baseline model.

Figure 3. Overview of the proposed hierarchy-aware HYPERSURG baseline model. Surgical video clips at three hierarchy levels (action, step, phase) are encoded by a TimeSformer (ViT-B/16), while the corresponding narration-derived captions are encoded by BERTbase. Both branches project into a shared 256-D Lorentz hyperboloid L256 c via learned projections and the exponential map. The contrastive loss Lcontr aligns video–text pairs via Lorentz distance (Equation (5)); the entailment loss Lentail enforces parent–child containment across hierarchy levels within the same cone (Equation (8)).

Figure 5. Where does each model get it right, and when wrong, how bad is the error? Each row shows a test frame with ground-truth labels and top-5 step predictions. Top two rows: HYPERSURG predicts the exact step while SurgCLIP∗ (β) predicts a cousin from a different phase. Row 3: HYPERSURG predicts the wrong step but stays within the correct phase (sibling, 0.004 margin), while SurgCLIP∗ (β) gets the exact step. Flat metrics treat both errors identically. Row 4: HYPERSURG predicts Idle, a cross-phase error on GraSP, consistent with its DAG-like hierarchy. Row 5 (subtree lock-in): HYPERSURG commits to the wrong phase subtree, with all five predictions from Jejunojejunal Anastomosis instead of the ground-truth Gastrojejunal Anastomosis, while SurgCLIP∗ (β) ranks the correct step first. Both the strengths and this failure mode are consistent with the same geometric property: hierarchical containment helps when the correct subtree is identified, but can trap the model when sibling phases are visually similar.

Table 3. Task 2: Cross-Level Consistency (%). Bold = best per dataset. As models become more hierarchy-aware, catastrophic failures where both levels are wrong decrease, and a correct phase prediction more often leads to a correct step, showing that the two granularity levels become coupled rather than independent.

Table 2. Task 1: Single- and Multi-Level Recognition. Zeroshot video-averaged accuracy (%), bold = best per dataset. Overall phase and step recognition both improve with hierarchyawareness, though per-dataset performance varies. The multi-level score, which requires both levels to be strong, tends to benefit from hierarchy-awareness, with gains scaling with tree-likeness.

Table 10. Sensitivity of HYPERSURG to the entailment loss weight λ (video-averaged accuracy, %). All variants use the full configuration (Lorentz + cones + triplet sampler), only λ varies. We select λ=0.1 as it yields the most balanced performance across both levels. Bold = best per dataset.

Table 8. Reimplementation validation. Zero-shot downstream performance (video-averaged, %) comparing the original SurgCLIP(β) results from Perez et al. [18] (their Table 2) with our reimplementation SurgCLIP∗ (β), trained on the same data with the same procedure.

Table 9. Ablation of HYPERSURG components (video-averaged accuracy, %). All variants use Lorentz distance. The full model achieves the best overall performance, with both components contributing complementary gains. Bold = best per dataset.

Figure 4. Per-level metrics cannot distinguish between errors. On both frames, each model predicts the correct phase but the wrong step, so accuracy and F1 record the same outcome. The errors differ in where they land in the hierarchy: the orange prediction is a sibling of the ground truth, a different step within the correct phase, while the red one is a cousin, from an unrelated phase. SURGHIBENCH measures this distinction.

Table 4. Task 3: Error severity (%). Bold = best per dataset. The hierarchy-aware model’s predictions more often fall within the correct phase and preserve the surgical action, indicating that its step predictions are more context-aware.
Table 7. Zero-shot prompts: MIPO steps (8 classes; see Tab. 6 caption).

Table 6. Zero-shot prompts: MIPO phases (5 classes). The MIPO repository documentation reports 4 phases and 6 steps; the released annotation files contain 5 and 8 distinct labels, respectively. We use the annotation file counts throughout.

Figure 2. Hyperbolic geometry organizes the surgical hierarchy by embedding norm; Euclidean cosine space collapses it. (a) In HYPERSURG (green), embedding norms increase from fine-grained actions to coarse phases, reflecting the hierarchical structure. Gray wedges are entailment cones (Equation (7)). (b) In SurgCLIP∗ (β) (red), L2 normalization for cosine similarity discards any norm signal, preventing cosine-based models from exploiting the hierarchy. Bottom: per-level norm distributions. Note distinguishability of hierarchical levels in hyperbolic space.
